cards.title: The 5 Arabic Negation Pairings
cards.summary: In Arabic, each time-frame locks onto its own negation particle — and that particle controls the verb ending.

diagram.danger: ✗ لَا + Past (لَا ذَهَبْتُ) = Wish / Curse (e.g. لَا قَدَّرَ اللهُ "May Allah forbid"), NEVER factual "didn't"!

rows.col4: Standard MSA & Qur'ān (لَمْ يَلِدْ وَلَمْ يُولَدْ)
Everyday spoken & written MSA
Habitual / right now
Future refusal / certainty
Noun / adjective sentences

cards.trap: Never pair لَا with a past verb for ordinary negation: ✗ لَا ذَهَبْتُ is ungrammatical for "I didn't go". Always use لَمْ أَذْهَبْ or مَا ذَهَبْتُ.

quickCheck.prompt: Say "I did not go to work" in BOTH valid Arabic ways — and remember why لَا ذَهَبْتُ is never used:
quickCheck.answerAr: لَمْ أَذْهَبْ إِلَى العَمَلِ  /  مَا ذَهَبْتُ إِلَى العَمَلِ
quickCheck.tr: lam adhhab ilā l-ʿamali  /  mā dhahabtu ilā l-ʿamali
quickCheck.answerEn: لَمْ + short present OR مَا + past verb (never ✗ لَا + past, which expresses a wish/curse).

cards.audioCue: Lesson card rule: Past negation uses lam plus short present, or maa plus past verb. Never pair laa with a past verb.

cards.title: How Arabic Marks Past, Present & Future
cards.summary: Past tense glues "who" onto the BACK of the root; Present glues "who" onto the FRONT; Future simply clips سَـ onto Present.

rows.col4: سَأَذْهَبُ (sa-adhhabu)
سَتَذْهَبُ (sa-tadhhabu)
سَيَذْهَبُ (sa-yadhhabu)
سَتَذْهَبُ (sa-tadhhabu)
سَنَذْهَبُ (sa-nadhhabu)
سَيَذْهَبُونَ (sa-yadhhabūna)

cards.trap: Don't mix front and back markers (never ✗ أَذْهَبْتُ) — and remember only THEY (هُمْ) takes the plural tail ـُونَ in present (يَذْهَبُونَ) and ـُوا in past (ذَهَبُوا); WE (نَحْنُ) is just نَـ with NO tail (نَذْهَبُ).

quickCheck.prompt: Flip "I read the Qur'an" across Past → Present → Future:
quickCheck.answerAr: قَرَأْتُ القُرْآنَ ← أَقْرَأُ القُرْآنَ ← سَأَقْرَأُ القُرْآنَ
quickCheck.tr: qaraʾtu l-qurʾāna → aqraʾu l-qurʾāna → sa-aqraʾu l-qurʾāna
quickCheck.answerEn: Past = suffix ـتُ (قَرَأْتُ); Present = prefix أَ (أَقْرَأُ); Future = سَـ + present (سَأَقْرَأُ).

cards.audioCue: Lesson card rule: Past tense puts the person ending on the back; present puts it on the front; future adds sa to the front of present.

cards.title: The 3 Arabic Words for "Price / Cost"
cards.summary: English says "price/cost" for almost everything; Arabic cleanly separates intrinsic value, shop rate, and service fare.

lanes.title: Intrinsic Value / Worth
lanes.desc: What an item is truly worth or paid for in exchange (Qur'ān & classic prose).

lanes.title: Market Sticker / Rate
lanes.desc: The listed shop price, menu rate, or market quote.

lanes.title: Service Fare / Rent / Wage
lanes.desc: Payment for transport, labour, or hiring space (never a physical object).

rows.col4: Handing money for goods; Qur'ān 2:41 (ثَمَنًا قَلِيلًا)
Asking how much something costs in a shop or market
Taxi rides, bus tickets, delivery fees (root أ-ج-ر ajr reward!)

cards.trap: Never ask a taxi driver for السِّعْر — ask كَمِ الأُجْرَةُ؟ ("How much is the fare?"). Notice أُجْرَة shares root أ-ج-ر with أَجْر (divine reward/wage).

quickCheck.prompt: Which word do you ask a shopkeeper vs a taxi driver?
quickCheck.answerAr: فِي السُّوقِ: كَمِ السِّعْرُ؟  /  فِي السَّيَّارَةِ: كَمِ الأُجْرَةُ؟
quickCheck.tr: kami s-siʿru (shop) vs kami l-ujratu (taxi fare)
quickCheck.answerEn: سِعْر = shop/market tag; أُجْرَة = taxi fare/service fee; ثَمَن = value/sum paid.

cards.audioCue: Lesson card rule: Use si-ir for a shop price, ujrah for a taxi fare or service fee, and thaman for intrinsic value.

cards.title: Pronoun Endings: Mine, For Me, & Him vs Her (-ka / -ki)
cards.summary: Arabic rarely leaves "my / me / your" as separate words — one tiny ending on a noun, preposition, or verb does the whole job.

lanes.title: 1st Person Attachment
lanes.desc: Noun + ـِي = my (كِتَابِي) · Prep + ـِي = for/with me (لِي / عِنْدِي) · Verb + ـنِي = me (سَاعَدَنِي)

lanes.title: Speaking to a Man
lanes.desc: Short fatḥah (-a): كَيْفَ حَالُكَ؟ · مَا اسْمُكَ؟ · هَلْ يُمْكِنُكَ؟

lanes.title: Speaking to a Woman (e.g. Saba)
lanes.desc: Short kasrah (-i): كَيْفَ كَانَ يَوْمُكِ؟ · هَلْ يُمْكِنُكِ؟ (Same spelling, vowel flips!)

rows.col4: Drop الـ when adding a possessive suffix
لِـ + ـِي = لِي (for me/mine); عِنْدَ + ـِي = عِنْدِي (I have)
Verbs insert a protective ن (nūn al-wiqāyah): ـنِي
ـكَ (-ka) to a man · ـكِ (-ki) to Saba / a woman

cards.trap: Never keep الـ on a word that has a possessive ending: say كِتَابِي (my book), never ✗ الكِتَابِي!

quickCheck.prompt: How do you ask Saba "How was your day?" vs asking a male colleague?
quickCheck.answerAr: لِزَوْجَتِكَ: كَيْفَ كَانَ يَوْمُكِ؟  /  لِلرَّجُلِ: كَيْفَ كَانَ يَوْمُكَ؟
quickCheck.tr: kayfa kāna yawmuki (-ki fem.) vs yawmuka (-ka masc.)
quickCheck.answerEn: ـكِ (-ki with kasrah) for her; ـكَ (-ka with fatḥah) for him.

cards.audioCue: Lesson card rule: Attach ee for my, nee after a verb for me, ka when speaking to a man, and ki when speaking to a woman.

cards.title: Possession (Idāfah) vs Noun + Adjective
cards.summary: Where الـ sits tells you everything: "the" on the SECOND word only = "X of the Y"; "the" on BOTH words = "the [adjective] X".

lanes.title: Possession Bridge (إِضَافَة)
lanes.desc: مِفْتَاحُ الغُرْفَةِ = "the key OF the room" (Word 1 is bare; Word 2 takes ـِ kasrah).

lanes.title: Noun + Adjective (نَعْت)
lanes.desc: الغُرْفَةُ الجَدِيدَةُ = "the new room" (Adjective comes AFTER noun & mirrors الـ, gender, case).

rows.col4: The key of the room
The prayer of Friday (Jumu'ah prayer)
The nearby mosque
Healthy food

cards.trap: Never say ✗ المِفْتَاحُ الغُرْفَةِ for "the room key" — the first word of an idāfah bridge NEVER wears الـ!

quickCheck.prompt: Say "the room key" in Arabic — where does الـ go?
quickCheck.answerEn: الـ goes ONLY on the second word (الغُرْفَةِ); مِفْتَاحُ stays bare.

cards.audioCue: Lesson card rule: In possession, only the second word takes al. When an adjective describes a noun, both words match.

cards.title: High-Value Minimal Pairs: One Dot Changes Everything
cards.summary: Locking look-alike pairs side-by-side stops silent mix-ups in both everyday speech and Qur'ānic listening.

lanes.title: أَعُودُ (Return) vs أَعُوذُ (Seek Refuge)
lanes.desc: Plain د (ع-و-د) = I return home · Dotted ذ (ع-و-ذ) = I seek refuge in Allah (Al-Falaq / An-Nās).

lanes.title: جَوْزَة (Walnut) vs زَوْجَة (Wife)
lanes.desc: ج leads the crunchy walnut snack (جَوْزَة) · ز leads your spouse/partner (زَوْجَة)!

lanes.title: حَفْلَة (Party) vs أُرَتِّبُ (I Tidy)
lanes.desc: حَفْلَة shares root with Bengali মাহফিল (mahfil gathering) · أُرَتِّبُ shares root with tartīb (neat order).

rows.col4: Plain د = return to your door; dotted ذ = أَعُوذُ بِاللَّهِ
ج first = Jawzah walnut; ز first = Zawjah wife
ḥaflah = social celebration (mahfil); ijtimāʿ = work meeting (root Jumu'ah)
taqabbala = Bengali কবুল (kobul accept); ʿabadtu = past of نَعْبُدُ

quickCheck.prompt: Contrast أَعُودُ vs أَعُوذُ — and what is the Jumu'ah prayer greeting "May Allah accept"?
quickCheck.answerAr: أَعُودُ (أَرْجِعُ إِلَى البَيْتِ) vs أَعُوذُ (بِاللهِ)  ·  تَقَبَّلَ اللهُ
quickCheck.tr: aʿūdu (return) vs aʿūdhu (seek refuge) · taqabbala llāh
quickCheck.answerEn: Plain د = return home; dotted ذ = seek refuge; تَقَبَّلَ اللهُ = May Allah accept (kobul).

cards.audioCue: Lesson card rule: Plain daal in a-oodu means I return home; dotted dhaal in a-oodhu means I seek refuge in Allah.

cards.title: Surah An-Nās Anatomy: Why الصُّدُور (Chests) and Not القُلُوب (Hearts)?
cards.summary: In Qur'ānic precision, the whisperer (الوَسْوَاس الخَنَّاس) can only pace the outer courtyard (الصَّدْر); he cannot enter the locked heart (القَلْب) unless invited.

diagram.outer: الصَّدْر (aṣ-ṣadr — Outer Courtyard / Chest): Where الوَسْوَاس الخَنَّاس throws passing whispers (يُوَسْوِسُ فِي صُدُورِ النَّاسِ).
diagram.shield: 🛡️ ذِكْرُ اللهِ (Remembrance of Allah): The instant you remember Allah, الخَنَّاس shrinks back & retreats!
diagram.inner: ❤️ القَلْب / الفُؤَاد (al-qalb — Inner Sanctuary / Heart): Seat of īmān — locked to Shayṭān unless the gate is opened.

rows.col4: Onomatopoeic rustle: repetitive, subtle inner muttering
Cowardly slinker: retreats upon dhikr, creeps back in heedlessness
Ṣudūr = outer foyer/chests (accessible to passing thoughts), NOT qulūb!
Tied knots (same root as ʿaqd contract & ʿaqīdah creed)

quickCheck.prompt: In Surah An-Nās, why does Allah say فِي صُدُورِ النَّاسِ (in the chests) rather than قُلُوب (hearts), and what makes الخَنَّاس retreat?
quickCheck.answerAr: الصَّدْرُ هُوَ السَّاحَةُ الخَارِجِيَّةُ، وَيَخْنِسُ الشَّيْطَانُ عِنْدَ ذِكْرِ اللهِ
quickCheck.answerEn: الصَّدْر (chest) is the outer courtyard around القَلْب (the heart), and الخَنَّاس slinks back whenever Allah is remembered.

cards.audioCue: Lesson card rule: In Surah An-Nas, whispers only reach as-sadr, the outer chest, and retreat the moment you remember Allah.

cards.title: The Polite Request & Conversation Control Ladder
cards.summary: Four reusable sentence frames let you ask for anything, request help politely, or slow a fast speaker down without switching to English.

rows.col4: أَحْتَاجُ always pairs with preposition إِلَى
Bridge word أَنْ flips verb ending from -u to -a
Bengali মুমকিন (mumkin) + hear AID in mu-sa-AID-ah!
Pair with لَمْ أَفْهَمْ، كَرِّرْ مِنْ فَضْلِكَ (I didn't understand, repeat please)

quickCheck.prompt: How do you politely ask "Can you help me?" and "Speak slowly, please" in Arabic?
quickCheck.answerAr: هَلْ يُمْكِنُكَ مُسَاعَدَتِي؟  ·  تَكَلَّمْ بِبُطْءٍ مِنْ فَضْلِكَ
quickCheck.tr: hal yumkinuka musāʿadatī? · takallam bi-buṭʾin min faḍlika
quickCheck.answerEn: يُمْكِنُكَ (mumkin) + مُسَاعَدَتِي (my aid); تَكَلَّمْ بِبُطْءٍ (speak with slowness).

cards.audioCue: Lesson card rule: Pair ahtaaju with ilaa for I need, ureedu an for I want to, and hal yumkinuka musaa-adatee for can you help me.

cards.title: The 7-Day Number Root Map & Telling Time
cards.summary: Five days of the Arabic week literally count 1 to 5 from Sunday, Friday means "Gathering", and clock hours use feminine ordinal adjectives.

nodes.sub: Same root as اجْتِمَاع (meeting) & مَسْجِد جَامِع

rows.col4: Sunday is for the Arabic lesson
Tomorrow is Friday (after day 5 الخَمِيس)
I wake up at 7 o'clock
I return at 8 o'clock

cards.trap: Exception on the clock: 1 o'clock uses الوَاحِدَة (السَّاعَةُ الوَاحِدَةُ), while 2:00–10:00 follow the clean الثَّانِيَة / الثَّالِثَة / السَّابِعَة / الثَّامِنَة pattern!

quickCheck.prompt: Why is Thursday called الخَمِيس and Friday called الجُمُعَة — and how do you say "at 7 o'clock"?
quickCheck.answerEn: Sunday–Thursday count 1–5 (أحد..خميس); الجُمُعَة = assembly (ج-م-ع); clock hours take feminine ordinals (السَّاعَةِ السَّابِعَةِ).

cards.audioCue: Lesson card rule: Sunday to Thursday count one to five, Friday means gathering, and clock hours use feminine ordinal numbers.

cards.title: The Qur'ān Glue & Pronoun Skeleton
cards.summary: Nearly a third of every surah is tiny prepositions and openers (فِي · عَلَى · لِ · مِنْ · بِ · إِنَّ · رَبّ) fused to pronoun tails (-hu, -hā, -hum, -kum, -nā). Peel the tail first to hear the root clearly.

lanes.title: فِيهَا · عَلَيْهِمْ
lanes.desc: fī-hā (in it) · ʿalay-him (upon them) — long vowel shifts (-ay-him) before -hum/-kum.

lanes.title: لَهُمْ · مِنْهُمْ
lanes.desc: la-hum (for them — li- opens to la-!) · min-hum (from / among them).

lanes.title: إِنَّهُمْ · رَبُّهُمْ
lanes.desc: inna-hum (indeed they) · rabbu-hum (their Sustainer) — opener or Lord fused directly to owner.

rows.col4: In it (the Garden) are raised couches — fī + hā = 1 word
The path of those You favoured upon them — ʿalā bends to ʿalay-
For them is an unfailing reward — li- opens to la- before pronouns
Indeed their Lord, about them, that Day is All-Aware

cards.trap: English hears 2–3 separate words ('in it', 'upon them', 'for them', 'indeed they'), so the ear hunts for a long obscure root inside عَلَيْهِمْ or إِنَّهُمْ. Peel -hu / -hā / -hum / -kum / -nā off the end first!

quickCheck.prompt: How does the Qur'ān fuse 'upon' (عَلَى) + 'them' (هُمْ) as one word in Al-Fātiḥah 1:7?
quickCheck.answerEn: عَلَى bends to عَلَيْـ before هِمْ: عَلَيْهِمْ (upon them).

cards.audioCue: Lesson Card: The Quran Glue Skeleton. Nearly a third of every surah is tiny glue words fused with pronoun tails: fiha means in it, alayhim means upon them, lahum means for them, minhum means from them, and innahum means indeed they. Whenever a word sounds long by ear, peel off hum, kum, ha, or hu first.

cards.title: Doer (فَاعِل) vs. Done-To (مَفْعُول) Ear Moulds
cards.summary: Arabic stamps its two biggest role-labels right onto the sound of a root: long ā after letter 1 (CāCiC) marks the active Doer, while starting with ma- plus long -ū- (maCCūC) marks the Done-To object.

lanes.title: حَاسِد · عَابِد · مَالِك
lanes.desc: Long ā right after the 1st root letter = the active Doer (envier · worshipper · master).

lanes.title: مَغْضُوب · مَرْفُوع · مَمْنُون
lanes.desc: Prefix ma- + long -ū- before the last root letter = Done-To (angered-upon · raised · cut off).

lanes.title: سَرِير ← سُرُر
lanes.desc: Short u-u reshapes familiar singular nouns into crisp Qur'ānic plurals (couch → couches).

rows.col4: And from the evil of an envier (ḥāsid = Doer) when he envies
Nor are you worshippers (ʿābidūn = Doers) of what I worship
Not those angered-upon (al-maghḍūb = Done-To) — strip ma- and -ū- to hear غ-ض-ب!
In it are couches (surur from سَرِير) raised high (marfūʿah = Done-To)

cards.trap: Never treat مَغْضُوب or مَرْفُوعَة as unrelated dictionary words! The 'مَـ' prefix is a sound-badge, not a root letter: strip ma- and -ū- and your ear hears غ-ض-ب (anger) and ر-ف-ع (raise) immediately.

quickCheck.prompt: You hear the 'ma-…-ū-' mould in مَرْفُوعَةٌ (88:13, root ر-ف-ع 'raise'). What does مَرْفُوعَةٌ mean?
quickCheck.answerEn: مَرْفُوعَةٌ uses the maCCūCah Done-To mould on ر-ف-ع ('raise') → 'raised high'.

cards.audioCue: Lesson Card: Doer versus Done-To Moulds. Long aa after the first letter marks the active Doer: hasid is an envier, abid is a worshipper, malik is a master. Starting with ma and ending with long oo marks Done-To: maghdub means angered upon, and marfuah means raised high.

cards.title: The Qur'ān Plural & Story Engine (-ū / -ūna)
cards.summary: Notice the Qur'ān switching effortlessly between 'I / he' and whole communities: past actions add -ū (آمَنُوا they believed), present groups wrap ya-…-ūna (they do) vs ta-…-ūna (you all do), and إِذَا flips past verbs into future certainty.

nodes.sub: āmanū · ʿamilū · qālū = they believed / did / said
Starts with يَـ (ya-) + ends -ūna = THEY know / worship
Starts with تَـ (ta-) + ends -ūna = YOU ALL know / worship

diagram.danger: After إِذَا ('when'), Arabic uses the PAST verb shape (إِذَا جَاءَ = 'when it comes') to portray a coming reality as already guaranteed.

rows.col4: Except those who believed and did righteous deeds (103:3)
No indeed! Soon you all will know (سَوْفَ + present)
I do not worship (aʿbudu) what you all worship (taʿbudūn)
When the help of Allah and victory comes (past shape = guaranteed)

cards.trap: In fast recitation, يَعْلَمُونَ (THEY know) and تَعْلَمُونَ (YOU ALL know) sound identical except for the very first letter: listen cleanly for y- vs t-!

quickCheck.prompt: Complete Sūrat al-ʿAṣr 103:3: إِلَّا الَّذِينَ ___ ('except those who believed' — past plural '-ū')

cards.audioCue: Lesson Card: The Quran Plural and Story Engine. Ending a past verb with long oo means they did: amanu is they believed, amilu is they did, qalu is they said. In the present, ya plus una means they do, while ta plus una means you all do: ya'lamuna is they know, ta'lamuna is you all know.

cards.title: Root Multiplier: 3 Verb Shifts That Unlock Hundreds of Ayahs
cards.summary: One 3-letter root multiplies cleanly: Form I is the base action (knew / came down), Form II/IV makes someone else do it (taught / sent down), and Form X 'ista- / nasta-' means earnestly seeking that root.

lanes.title: عَلِمَ · نَزَلَ · غَفَرَ
lanes.desc: Plain root = base action: knew · came down · forgave.

lanes.title: عَلَّمَ · أَنْزَلَ
lanes.desc: Doubled middle letter (ـلّـ) OR 'a-' prefix (أَـ) = He taught (caused to know) · He sent down.

lanes.title: اِسْتَغْفَرَ · نَسْتَعِينُ
lanes.desc: Prefix '-st-' (ista- / nasta-) = earnestly seek / ask for the root (forgiveness · help).

rows.col4: He taught (ʿallama, II) man what he did not know (yaʿlam, I) — 1 root ع-ل-م!
Indeed We sent it down (anzalnā-hu, IV) — causative of نَزَلَ (came down)
Glorify your Lord's praise and seek His forgiveness (istaghfir-hu, X from غ-ف-ر)
You alone we worship (Form I) and You alone we seek help (nastaʿīn, X)

cards.trap: Don't learn عَلِمَ (knew), عَلَّمَ (taught), أَنْزَلَ (sent down), and اسْتَغْفَرَ (seek forgiveness) as four unrelated words. Your ear only needs the sound marker: middle shaddah (taught), 'a-' front (sent down), '-st-' front (seek).

quickCheck.prompt: In Al-ʿAlaq 96:5, يَعْلَمْ means 'he knows' — what Form II verb from the same ع-ل-م root means 'He TAUGHT'?
quickCheck.answerEn: Double the middle root letter لّ: عَلَّمَ (ʿallama = He taught).

cards.audioCue: Lesson Card: Three Verb Shifts That Multiply Every Root. Doubling the middle letter or adding an a prefix makes a root causative: alima means he knew, allama means He taught; nazala means came down, anzala means sent down. Adding ista or nasta means seeking: ghafara is forgave, istaghfir is seek forgiveness, and nasta'inu in Fatiha means we seek help.

cards.title: How Every Friday Khutbah Unfolds
cards.summary: A Friday khutbah is not an unpredictable lecture — it marches through 5 fixed Arabic signposts by ear: Opening Praise & Taqwā, the pivot 'أَمَّا بَعْدُ', Pause & 2nd Khutbah, Ṣalawāt & Du'ās (ending 'آمِينَ'), and Closing Āyah '16:90' + 'وَأَقِمِ الصَّلَاةَ'.

nodes.ar: الحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ ... يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اتَّقُوا اللَّهَ
nodes.sub: Khuṭbat al-Ḥājah — praising Allah + taqwā verses
Opening ends -> main Friday message starts right here

nodes.ar: أَقُولُ قَوْلِي هَذَا ... إِنَّ اللَّهَ وَمَلَائِكَتَهُ يُصَلُّونَ عَلَى النَّبِيِّ
nodes.sub: Imam sits, then returns for ṣalawāt & congregational du'ās

nodes.ar: إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَأْمُرُ بِالعَدْلِ وَالإِحْسَانِ ... وَأَقِمِ الصَّلَاةَ
nodes.sub: Remember Allah (2:152), then stand for iqāmah

diagram.danger: Ear cue: Do NOT tune out during the fast opening Arabic! Wait for أَمَّا بَعْدُ ('now then') and عِبَادَ اللَّهِ ('O servants of Allah') — that is where today's topic begins.

rows.col4: Truly the most truthful speech is the Book of Allah
Now then / as for what follows

rows.ar: إِنَّ اللَّهَ وَمَلَائِكَتَهُ يُصَلُّونَ عَلَى النَّبِيِّ
rows.tr: inna llāha wa-malāʾikatahu yuṣallūna ʿalā n-nabiyy
rows.col4: Indeed Allah & His angels send blessings upon the Prophet
Indeed Allah commands justice and excellence
And establish the prayer

cards.trap: Notice أَقِمِ الصَّلَاةَ at the very end takes a kasrah on مِ (wa-aqimi ṣ-ṣalāh) only because the next word starts with silent alif-lām — it is still a bare imperative command to the mu'adhdhin!

quickCheck.prompt: What does أَمَّا بَعْدُ signal in a khutbah — and what are the final words telling everyone the iqāmah is next?
quickCheck.tr: ammā baʿdu (topic starts) · wa-aqimi ṣ-ṣalāh (establish the prayer)
quickCheck.answerEn: أَمَّا بَعْدُ pivots from opening praise to today's topic; وَأَقِمِ الصَّلَاةَ closes the khutbah right before iqāmah.

cards.audioCue: Lesson Card: How Every Friday Khutbah Unfolds. Every khutbah follows five landmarks you can hear by ear. First the khatib praises Allah and recites the taqwa verses calling O you who believe. Second comes amma ba'du, which literally means now then and marks the exact start of today's topic. Third, he sits briefly and opens the second khutbah, reciting inna llaha wa mala'ikatahu to trigger blessings on the Prophet followed by community du'as ending in Amin. Finally, he closes with inna llaha ya'muru bil-adli wal-ihsan and wa-aqimi s-salah, signalling everyone to stand for prayer.

cards.title: The Du'ā & Imam Command Kit
cards.summary: Du'ās and imam announcements run on two grammatical switches you already know: direct vocative + bare command when calling Allah (رَبَّنَا ... آتِنَا / اِغْفِرْ), and plural -ū commands (اِسْتَوُوا / أَقِيمُوا) when the imam directs the rows.

lanes.title: رَبَّنَا / رَبِّ / اللَّهُمَّ + فِعْلُ أَمْر
lanes.desc: rabbana ātinā (grant us!) · rabbi zidnī (increase me!) · allāhumma ghfir (forgive!) — vocative drops the ي.

lanes.title: اِسْتَوُوا · تَقَدَّمُوا · سُدُّوا · أَقِيمُوا
lanes.desc: Plural command ending -ū means 'you all [do it]!' — straight rows, step forward, close gaps.

lanes.title: قَدْ قَامَتِ الصَّلَاةُ · رَبَّنَا وَلَكَ الحَمْدُ
lanes.desc: Fixed congregation cues for iqāmah, rising from rukūʿ, sajdah tilāwah, and 4 takbīrs in janāzah.

rows.col4: Our Lord, grant us good in this world (2:201)
My Lord, increase me in knowledge (20:114)

rows.ar: اللَّهُمَّ إِنَّكَ عَفُوٌّ تُحِبُّ العَفْوَ فَاعْفُ عَنِّي
rows.tr: allāhumma innaka ʿafuwwun tuḥibbu l-ʿafwa fa-ʿfu ʿannī
rows.col4: O Allah, You are Pardoning, You love pardon, so pardon me
Make the prayer rows straight
Our Lord, and to You belongs all praise

cards.trap: Don't look for يَا ('O!') inside اللَّهُمَّ or رَبَّنَا — اللَّهُمَّ puts ـمَّ at the end instead of يَا, and رَبِّ ('my Lord') drops its trailing ي in supplication for immediacy.

quickCheck.prompt: Translate by ear: رَبِّ زِدْنِي عِلْمًا — and explain the ending of أَقِيمُوا الصُّفُوفَ:
quickCheck.answerEn: 'My Lord, increase me in knowledge' (زِدْ command + ـنِي me); أَقِيمُوا uses plural -ū ('you all straighten the rows!').

cards.audioCue: Lesson Card: The Du'a and Imam Command Kit. Almost every du'a opens with Rabbi meaning my Lord, Rabbana meaning our Lord, or Allahumma meaning O Allah, followed immediately by a bare Arabic command such as ighfir meaning forgive or zidni meaning increase me. When the imam faces the congregation, he switches to plural commands ending in u: istawu means stand straight, taqaddamu means step forward, and aqimu s-sufuf means straighten the rows. Knowing those two command switches unlocks both du'a and live masjid speech.

cards.title: Past → Present Verb Patterns: The 3 Engines
cards.summary: Past-to-present changes follow 3 simple engines: plain 3-letter roots squeeze the 1st vowel silent (ذَهَبَ ← يَذْهَبُ); doubled-middle or أَ- verbs flip to يُـ / أُ (عَلَّمَ ← يُعَلِّمُ, أَرَادَ ← يُرِيدُ); and تَـ verbs keep their تَـ (تَعَلَّمَ ← يَتَعَلَّمُ).

lanes.title: Plain 3-Letter Root (Form I)
lanes.desc: Past: 3 open beats (dha-ha-ba). Present: snap أَ / تَ / يَ / نَ on front and squeeze letter 1 silent (a-dh-habu). Middle vowel (a / i / u) comes by ear.

lanes.title: "Yu-" Engine (Forms II & IV)
lanes.desc: Doubled middle (عَلَّمَ / رَتَّبَ) or opening أَ (أَرَادَ / أَنْزَلَ) ALWAYS flips the front vowel to يُـ / أُ (yu- / u-) and drops the 2nd vowel to -i- (يُعَلِّمُ, يُرِيدُ).

lanes.title: "Ta-" & "Ista-" Keepers (Forms V & X)
lanes.desc: Verbs starting with تَـ (تَعَلَّمَ / تَنَاوَلَ) KEEP تَـ after أَ/يَ (يَتَعَلَّمُ / أَتَعَلَّمُ). Verbs starting with اِسْتَـ (اِسْتَيْقَظَ) drop i- and snap أَ/يَ (يَسْتَيْقِظُ).

rows.ar: ذَهَبَ إِلَى العَمَلِ ← أَذْهَبُ إِلَى العَمَلِ

rows.col4: رَتَّبَ ← أُرَتِّبُ (tidy) · صَلَّى ← أُصَلِّي (pray)
أَنْزَلَ ← يُنْزِلُ (sent down) · أَعْطَى ← يُعْطِي (gave)
تَنَاوَلَ ← أَتَنَاوَلُ (had breakfast) · تَكَلَّمَ ← أَتَكَلَّمُ
اِسْتَغْفَرَ ← أَسْتَغْفِرُ (ask forgiveness)

cards.trap: On a تَـ verb like تَعَلَّمَ, saying "you/she learns" stacks TWO t's: تَتَعَلَّمُ (tataʿallamu). And never force yu- onto plain 3-letter verbs — yu- is the exclusive badge of Engine 2 (doubled middle عَلَّمَ or أَ- start أَرَادَ)!

quickCheck.prompt: Flip these three verbs from Past (he) → Present (I): ذَهَبَ · تَعَلَّمَ · أَرَادَ
quickCheck.answerAr: ذَهَبَ ← أَذْهَبُ  ·  تَعَلَّمَ ← أَتَعَلَّمُ  ·  أَرَادَ ← أُرِيدُ
quickCheck.tr: dhahaba → adhhabu · taʿallama → ataʿallamu · arāda → urīdu
quickCheck.answerEn: Plain 3-letter root = a- (أَذْهَبُ); تَـ verb keeps ta- (أَتَعَلَّمُ); أَ- Form IV flips to u-/yu- (أُرِيدُ).

cards.audioCue: Lesson card rule: Arabic verbs follow three main engines from past to present. Plain three-letter roots like dhahaba squeeze the first letter silent to adhhabu. Doubled middle or opening alif verbs like allama or arada flip to yu or u, giving yurid or uridu. And ta-verbs like ta-allama keep their ta, becoming yata-allamu or ata-allamu.

cards.title: 8 Core Persons vs All 14 Arabic Persons
cards.summary: Classical Arabic has 14 pronoun slots, but our 8-person core (أَنَا · أَنْتَ · أَنْتِ · هُوَ · هِيَ · نَحْنُ · أَنْتُمْ · هُمْ) already covers ~97% of everyday speech — including feminine أَنْتِ for Saba! Duals and feminine plurals wait for recognition by ear.

lanes.title: Speak First (Master These)
lanes.desc: أَنَا · أَنْتَ · أَنْتِ · هُوَ · هِيَ · نَحْنُ · أَنْتُمْ · هُمْ — covers every normal conversation, including أَنْتِ (you, f.) for Saba.

lanes.title: هُمَا / أَنْتُمَا (Recognise by Ear)
lanes.desc: Used only for literally 2 people (ـَا / ـَانِ). Frequent in the Qur'ān (رَبِّكُمَا in Ar-Raḥmān), rare in early speaking.

lanes.title: هُنَّ / أَنْتُنَّ (Qur'ān & Formal)
lanes.desc: All-female group of 3+ (ـنَ). Any mixed group (even 1 man + 10 women) defaults to هُمْ / أَنْتُمْ.

columns: Do I Need to Learn It Now?

rows.col4: YES (already in Core 8!) — use with Saba & female tutors
YES (already in Core 8!) — mixed or male groups
Ear only for now — literally 2 people
Qur'ān ear cue (Ar-Raḥmān 55:13 — dual -kumā / -ān)
Ear only for now — all-female 3+ (also أَنْتُنَّ)

cards.trap: No, 8 persons is NOT too short — every core verb table on this site already includes أَنْتِ (you, female, row #8)! Just don't skip row #8 when speaking to Saba (هَلْ ذَهَبْتِ؟ / كَيْفَ كَانَ يَوْمُكِ؟). Save dual (هُمَا / أَنْتُمَا) and feminine plural (هُنَّ / أَنْتُنَّ) for ear recognition until the Core 8 are automatic.

quickCheck.prompt: Ask Saba (you, fem.) "Did you go?" vs Ask a mixed group "Did they go?":
quickCheck.answerEn: أَنْتِ takes -ti (ذَهَبْتِ) in past and -īna (تَذْهَبِينَ) in present; mixed groups use هُمْ (-ū / -ūna).

cards.audioCue: Lesson card rule: Classical Arabic has fourteen pronoun slots, but our core eight already cover ninety seven percent of everyday speech, including feminine anti for speaking to your wife. Dual huma and antuma, plus feminine plural hunna, are for recognition by ear until the core eight are automatic.
